📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports.

The international break is over as domestic football boogies back. Primed to feel the force is Dominic Booth at the helm of our essential gateway to the weekend’s action. Saturday offers a magnificent seven Premier League matches, bookended by Manchester City v Fulham and Newcastle v Arsenal. There is also a full programme of Championship, League One, and League Two fixtures, plus Celtic and Rangers taking to the Glasgow greensward in Scotland. In the WSL, Liverpool host Chelsea before rich kids London City prepare to receive Crystal Palace. For breaking news, reader input and good vibes aplenty – join the conversation at matchday.live@theguardian.com.

According to recent reports, to the background buzz of Australian cricket ripping itself apart over sandpapergate, England kick off their T20 series at the same venue they became world champions four years ago. The Melbourne Cricket Ground has not always been a happy hunting ground for touring England sides but Harry Brook’s last two visits as captain have been triumphant. A two-day win at the 90,000-capacity venue in last year’s Boxing Day Test was not only the high point of a traumatic Ashes campaign; it was their first red-ball victory on Australian soil since 2011. MCG also hosted England’s T20 World Cup triumph in 2022, where Brook was part of the side that defeated Pakistan to lift the trophy behind enemy lines. Rob Smyth has over-by-over coverage with Ali Martin reporting from Melbourne.

It has been revealed that the lunchtime kick-off is a vital one for the hosts. City have wobbled of late, three straight Premier League defeats leave the beleaguered club in third with 21 points from the first 10 games of Enzo Maresca’s tenure. In stark contrast, the Cottagers are unbeaten in their last four games, after four defeats and two draws in their first six. Wins over Hull and Coventry came before draws with Aston Villa and Newcastle. Barry Glendenning helms the blog as Will Unwin reports from the Etihad Stadium.

England are have been transformed since stumbling through the Six Nations and then falling to South Africa at Ellis Park, winning four consecutive Tests, amassing 36 tries and addressing their disciplinary lapses. Aided by thumping victories over Fiji and Japan, they have rebuilt impressively to secure a shot at reaching the Nations Championship final, but New Zealand provide the true measure of their progress. Only South Africa are higher in the rankings and a year out from the 2027 World Cup final, it is the opportunity for Steve Borthwick’s men to make a statement. Lee Calvert blogs the action and the trio of Robert Kitson, Andy Bull and Gerard Meagher making up our Twickenham reporting team.

Katy Murrells is at the controls of our tennis liveblog as the semi-finals pan out in Turin. The first session starts at 2.30pm, with the evening match due to start at about 8.30pm.

Emillia Hawkins keeps the updates flowing on the five afternoon kick-offs: Aston Villa v Sunderland, Bournemouth v Nottingham Forest, Chelsea v Leeds, Coventry v Crystal Palace, and Tottenham v Ipswich – the pick of the bunch. Roberto De Zerbi seemed to be making an impact at Spurs before a defeat by Leeds tripped up his side. Their record is grim against the Tractor Boys: four defeats in their last five Premier league games.

Lee Calvert is back on deck as Ireland risk a Springbok backlash from a side bruised by defeat by France and furious at their coach, Rassie Erasmus, for getting banned after his incendiary “match-fixing” comments. There is more at stake in this November’s meeting between the sides than last year’s chaotic Test. The Irish were down to 12 men at one stage and the Springboks won 24-13 for their first win in Dublin since 2012. Both countries are still in the running to top their respective pools and play in the final on Finals weekend at Twickenham. Brendan Fanning reports.

Sources indicate that city’s slump has allowed the defending champions, Arsenal, to seize early control and they will hope to continue their relentless start to the season. They head to Newcastle where a toxic reception awaits Bruno Guimarães as he returns to Tyneside in Arsenal colours for the first time since his summer move. The Gunners are five points clear of second-placed Brighton at the top after winning nine of their first 10 games. Matthias Jaissle’s inconsistent hosts have managed just one win in their past five league matches, losing to Everton and Aston Villa along the way. Join Rob Smyth for MBM commentary, with Louis Taylor reporting.

Kimi Antonelli may have already won the drivers’ crown, but second place in the standings is still up for grabs and Max Verstappen can tighten his grip in Sin City. The Red Bull driver is 17 points clear of Mercedes’ George Russell, who moved back up to third place, one point ahead of Lewis Hamilton after his fourth place at Interlagos. Krishani Dhanji be live blogging the race in the small hours, with Giles Richards reporting from Las Vegas.

Dominic Booth and Emillia Hawkins clock on with all the latest news and reader views for a Sunday featuring the Premier League fixture of the weekend. Mauricio Pochettino takes charge of Manchester United at Anfield just days after wrapping up his reign as USA men’s coach. Victory would give him instant momentum as he fights to lift the club up the table. Earlier, hard-charging Brighton will fancy their chances against Hull, who have not won a Premier League match since August. For breaking news, reader input and good vibes aplenty – join the conversation at matchday.live@theguardian.com.

It has been revealed that emillia Hawkins and John Brewin keep track of Sunday’s WSL fixtures from midday as Birmingham face Manchester United and Charlton host Aston Villa. Then it is Everton v Brighton at 2pm followed by a London derby as Rita Guarino’s in-form West Ham visit Arsenal, with the Irons having notched four wins in their past five matches in all competitions. The Gunners are toiling, and they sit sixth in the standings going into the weekend, with just three wins from their opening 10 matches.

Sources indicate that second-placed Brighton have become the most unlikely title contenders with their free-scoring football and have every chance of continuing to defy the sceptics as they take on Hull. The Seagulls are the league’s top scorers with 26 goals, 11 more than Arsenal, and have the second-tightest defence, with just seven goals conceded.Join Dominic Booth for minute-by-minute coverage, with Aaron Bower reporting from MKM Stadium.

Rob Smyth buckles up for the big one at Anfield with all eyes on the latest United manager, Mauricio Pochettino. United’s tally of eight points and one win after 10 games is their lowest at this stage of a league season for 40 years. The former Southampton, Spurs and Chelsea manager says he needs time to turn the dysfunctional club’s fortunes around but he will be aware of the need to show progress quickly, with Liverpool in no mood to offer their most bitter rivals any favours. Looking for omens? The Argentinian’s first game for Chelsea was against Liverpool, which ended in a 1-1 draw at Stamford Bridge. Andy Hunter and Jamie Jackson make up our reporting team on Merseyside.

Daniel Harris offers live coverage of the final from Turin as the season-ending indoor hard-court tournament featuring the top eight singles players and top eight doubles teams draws to a thrilling close.

According to recent reports, graham Searles returns with his essential NFL liveblog covering the seven 6pm clashes. The division-leading Buffalo Bills (8-1), who boast the top scoring offence and second-best rush attack in the NFL, meet the Miami Dolphins (1-8) in the big AFC East clash. The other early Sunday games are Bears v Saints, Lions v Buccaneers, Panthers v Ravens, Cowboys v Titans, Chiefs v Cardinals, and Eagles v Steelers.

Arsenal 'have ingredients' but Europe's elite on another level

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arsenal goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez made six saves but was beaten twice in defeat by Lyon.
  • It is only 18 months since Arsenal tasted European glory, but they are not a team on many people's list of favourites for this season's Women's Champions League.
  • That is because not only have the Gunners disappointed across their opening 15 matches of the season, but also the elite teams in Europe seem to have gone up another level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez made six saves but was beaten twice in defeat by Lyon.

It is only 18 months since Arsenal tasted European glory, but they are not a team on many people's list of favourites for this season's Women's Champions League.

That is because not only have the Gunners disappointed across their opening 15 matches of the season, but also the elite teams in Europe seem to have gone up another level.

In the space of seven days, Arsenal have witnessed first hand what it takes to reach those heights - and the gap they must bridge.

Last week, they were resilient at Barcelona to earn a very respectable 1-1 draw, but were fortunate the Spanish side were not clinical with their chances at Camp Nou.

On Thursday night, they were outplayed at home in losing 2-0 to an excellent Lyon side, who look on course to match or better their runner-up finish from last season.

One point from such games could be pleasing - but that only reveals the work Arsenal need to do to be considered one of the top teams in Europe.

French giants Lyon outclass Arsenal in Women's Champions League.

Arsenal came into Thursday's defeat by Lyon off the back of a fifth successive Women's Super League draw at Emirates Stadium against London City Lionesses.

In contrast, Lyon have been flying domestically, winning all nine of their matches, scoring 49 goals, and then not conceding any in their unbeaten Champions League run.

Such form sets the pace and it was clear at Meadow Park that they were superior to Arsenal in every department.

Vibrant Germany international Jule Brand gave them the lead midway through the first half and Melchie Dumornay sealed the win with a powerful strike in the 57th minute.

Arsenal defender Leah Williamson said the "better team won the game" and manager Renee Slegers highlighted the difference in physicality between the teams.

"Compared to last year when we played Lyon [in the semi-finals], they are even better now. They have standout individual quality," Slegers stated.

Sources indicate that "They dominated in the first half. We had solutions for the second half and had more presence. We wore them down better but it still didn't lead to open chances.".

Despite playing at right-back, Jule Brand had the third most touches in the Arsenal penalty area for Lyon (five) after striker Marie-Antoinette Katoto and fellow goalscorer Melchie Dumornay.

Recent findings suggest that lyon had a 3.33 expected goals ratio on Thursday, serving up 23 shots to Arsenal's seven. They created six big chances and 14 of their shots were inside the box.

Dumornay oozed quality, midfielder Lily Yohannes showed composure and Brand was very impressive both defensively and going forward for Lyon, deployed in a new position.

Those individuals have benefitted from the expertise of former Barcelona manager Jonatan Giraldez, who joined in June 2025 - the month after Arsenal won the Champions League - and has now had the time he needed to impose his style.

As a result, Lyon have gone up another level and the gap between these two teams has widened by Arsenal's drop-off this season.

Slegers also noted Arsenal had "prepared all we could" for the intensity that Lyon brought in London - but it still did not have an impact.

Asked how far off Lyon they right now are, Slegers noted: "It's 2-0 today and they are better than us but it doesn't mean if we were to play them again soon, this season, that it would be the same game again.

"We saw moments where we did well and we know from the last couple of years we can hurt Lyon.

Industry observers note that "But for today, their pace and physicality helped them get too much dominance in the game and that is one of their strengths. Then it became hard for us.".

Arsenal have not yet qualified for the knockout stages of the Champions League.

Williamson said Arsenal "know what they need to do to be better" and that they are aware of "where the gaps are" to Europe's elite.

They are already 12 points off the pace in the Women's Super League title race and are unlikely to qualify automatically for the Champions League quarter-finals.

"The level rises year on year. Everybody cops goals - we have to try not to and we have to create," remarked Williamson following the defeat by Lyon.

"We're all focused and we're all together. That's the most comforting thing for me - but this has been a tough period.".

It has not all been bad despite disappointing results - and context is important.

Over a gruelling seven days, they have faced European holders Barcelona, WSL high-flyers London City Lionesses and record Champions League winners Lyon.

They showed grit and resilience out in Barcelona last week - traits that have not been on show enough for Arsenal this season, but are clearly there.

Players like Williamson, striker Alessia Russo and summer signings Georgia Stanway and Ona Batlle know what it takes to compete at the highest level.

Arsenal invested in the summer transfer window and brought in proven, experienced players, but that has not translated into results - yet.

Giraldez stated time with his players has helped improve Lyon and perhaps that is what Arsenal need - patience.

"I think they are changing now. They made a good game against Barcelona and it's very difficult to go there and get a point," noted Giraldez.

"The game against London City was much better. It's not just about them, but also about us. Now we have improved and play better football than last year.

"I think it is a matter of time [for Arsenal]. They have a good coach and good players. In general, they have all the ingredients to have a good season.".

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed.

Tries: Piccardo (17), Matera (72) Conversions: Albornoz (18,73) Penalties: Albornoz (24).

France vs Argentina Nations Championship 8:10pm Saturday 21st November.

France reached the Nations Championship final after beating Argentina 45-17 with seven tries on Saturday.

England's 37-12 win against New Zealand left France needing a bonus-point victory to make the November 29 final against South Africa, who topped the southern hemisphere group despite losing to Ireland.

Already leading 21-10, Emilien Gailleton got France's fourth try for the bonus point in the 64th minute against 14 men, and moments later the yellow card for Pumas prop Mayco Vivas was upgraded to red.

France finished with three more tries. Lock Tyler Duguid charged through following an attacking lineout, centre Kalvin Gourgues revealed stunning pace from near halfway to make the left corner, and Louis Bielle-Biarrey completed the rout with his 31st try in 30 tests.

In the first half lock Mickaël Guillard and try-scoring hooker Peato Mauvaka crossed for France. Returning fly-half Matthieu Jalibert cleverly set up silky centre Gourgues shortly after the break for the first of his two tries.

Argentina led briefly at 10-7 for 10 minutes thanks to a converted try from centre Justo Piccardo and a penalty from fly-half Tomas Albornoz.

Jalibert's faster than expected recovery from a torn thigh allowed captain Antoine Dupont to resume at scrum-half after wearing the No 10 jersey a week ago against South Africa.

Dupont indicated his class at the end with a kick down the left flank for Bielle-Biarrey's try.

Gourdes nailed five conversions as a makeshift kicker on the night.

Tributes were held before the game for Federico Martín Aramburú, the former Argentina player who died four years ago after being fatally shot in Paris.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:.

According to recent reports, we'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow, thank you for staying with us. Tschüss!

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.

Pistorius said ‌criticism of ​Ukraine's deep strikes in ​Russia was ​misplaced.

In particular, Pistorius responded to US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby, who noted Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war.".

The German defense minister noted "criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military and military-used targets" was "quite a ​stupid thing.".

"Instead ‌of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on... energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius noted.

He added that attacks inside ⁠Russia ​against ​non-civilian targets ​and sites used ‌by the military ​are ⁠legal and legitimate targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Former US President Joe Biden's fresh autobiography "Promise Me, America" hit bookshelves on Tuesday, and it features anecdotes about several global leaders, including former German Chancellor Angela Merkel.

In the book, Biden dished on conversations that he and Merkel had about his predecessor and later successor, Donald Trump.

Citing conversations from early 2021, Biden wrote, "Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts.".

"She also wondered," wrote Biden, "why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel.".

Merkel and Trump were often at odds over challenges tied to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's dependence on Russian energy but one of the most infamous meetings between two came in the Oval Office in March 2017, when Trump awkwardly refused to shake hands with the German leader during a press availability despite photographers loudly encouraging him to do so.

Merkel reflected on the moment in her own 2024 memoir "Freedom" saying that after initially approaching Trump as someone "completely normal" she rapidly sensed that he viewed their public meetings as a kind of "you or me" competition.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a plan by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers ​to a deportation hub ​in ‌Rwanda.

Türk stated he had not yet ‌seen the draft proposal ‌but that ​his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by ​the proposed transfer of people from five ⁠European Union ​countries to ​Rwanda, where they have no ​genuine connection and ‌which has its own set ​of ⁠human rights challenges.".

Instead, he called ⁠for ​a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights.".

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the prepares would end in a "shipwreck" (see entry below).

Latest figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.

Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.

In a recent development, france was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.

The Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.

Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%)  had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.

Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.

Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.

The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.

VC noted that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.

Recent findings suggest that "The ball is now in the employer's court," VC mentioned in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.

Lufthansa, meanwhile, remarked it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 new cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.

VC noted it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.

The airline also said arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.

The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.

Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.

The ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.

The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, noted the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.

The ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.

Spranger said the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.

A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.

The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl remarked on Tuesday that the prepares would end in a "shipwreck.".

Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp stated that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.

"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he mentioned.

"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support.".

In a statement issued after the announcement of the looks, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.

"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.

"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it said.

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.

"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.

"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals.".

The announcement of the aims comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.

According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

The plan to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion,  German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius declared on Tuesday.

He noted that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.

Most of the new funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius said in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.

He said Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously declared, as well as newly introduced radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.

He also said that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.

Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.

He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.

"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.

He said Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.

Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he remarked meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and newly introduced transport links.

Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.

He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.

In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.

Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.

The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.

The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.

Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that  sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.

The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the Fresh York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.

Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents.".

It also stated that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank.".

The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.

The commission noted stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.

The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.

Some 286,000 new businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).

The BVR said the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.

However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.

In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.

The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.

The association also noted that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.

Prepares announced by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.

Migration hard-liner Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, one of the main advocates of the strategy, has, however, given assurances that it will be executed "in line with human rights" and "in accordance with European and German law.".

Meanwhile, more new businesses are expected to open in Germany this year than has been the case since 2015, a rise partly driven by the growing presence of artificial intelligence.

And internal documents leaked by whistleblowers from Deutsche Bank, a lender that has had more than its fair share of scandals in the past, have exposed more cases of malpractice and misconduct in recent years, media say.

Germany forward on her latest life in London and drawing strength from the memory of her late brother, Dennis.

It has been revealed that lisa Baum is 19, for the next few days at least, but you wouldn’t know it. The Germany forward plays with a maturity that explains why she was handed her Arsenal debut in their opening game of the season, less than two months after joining.

Baum had been told that the 2025 European champions had a vision for her but that coming in as a young player she would have to be patient. Ten minutes into her debut against Brighton, in Crawley, the young winger scored what would be the winning goal.

“It was unbelievable,” indicates Baum, speaking in a small meeting room at Arsenal’s London Colney training ground with a maturity that matches her play. “Everything just went so quick. I just shot, my brain was just switched off, it just came out.”.

That win kickstarted Arsenal’s season but it quickly stalled. In the league, the team went five games without a win. After a 2-0 defeat by OL Lyonnes in the Champions League on Thursday night, Arsenal have five wins from their opening 15 games. It is far from the season they, or many others, envisaged.

Sunday’s final home game of the year, against West Ham, offers an opportunity to take some positivity into the international break, after which Arsenal face three away fixtures before the winter pause.

It has been revealed that “I believe in us,” indicates Baum. “I think it’s all about the small margins. Sometimes it’s luck, sometimes it’s in the final decision-making, sometimes it’s how close we are to a goal that doesn’t go in. But we work really hard in every training session and on trying to keep ourselves up mentally and physically. We’re trying to push through the barrier that we maybe have right now, but we get a lot of trust from the staff and coaches. Everybody really believes in each other and I think it’s not going to take long before we’re through this part of the journey.”.

Recent findings suggest that overall, Arsenal have not been playing particularly badly. They have been creating chances and dominating games but struggling to translate that into goals and points. In October, Baum earned a first senior Germany call-up and made her debut off the bench at half-time against Australia, having previously featured for teams from the under-16s to under-23s.

The Liverpool head coach, Gareth Taylor, says Pro Ref has accepted it made an error in disallowing a goal his side thought they had scored during this month's 2-1 defeat by Arsenal at Anfield.

Sources indicate that the Women’s Super League game was level at 1-1 when Jenna Clark tucked the ball into the net after ­Arsenal had failed to clear a corner, but the assistant referee disallowed the goal for offside against Vivien ­Endemann. Replays highlighted the delivery had been ­inadvertently played off an Arsenal foot rather than being a deliberate forward pass from the home side. There is no VAR in the WSL.

Taylor, whose side host Chelsea in the WSL on Saturday, mentioned on Friday: “We have had an acceptance of a mistake from the corner that we scored from, where we should be 2-1 up at half-time. [There was] no apology, but we accept that there was an error made on their part and that game can look different.” Tom Garry.

Industry observers note that baum moved to Germany when she was four. Born to a Tanzanian mother and German father, she spent her first years in Dar es Salaam in Tanzania. They swapped a city with a population of about four million for Ahrensbök, a municipality with a population of just over 8,000 near the Baltic coast. “I think my mum had the hardest time out of us in the family, with the move to Germany,” she indicates. Baum says she and her brother, Dennis, “learned to adapt easily”.

Baum doesn’t remember her years on the east coast of Africa but when she went back three or four years ago, some sort of memory was triggered. “It was a feeling, or feelings,” she says. “It was so good to grow up there. It was warm, it was the beautiful beaches, it was having all your family around. I was in kindergarten or I was in the water a lot – I love to swim.”.

Sources indicate that she started playing football after the move to northern Germany, desperate to copy Dennis. “My father played football when he was younger – he was a goalkeeper – but he stopped when he didn’t really enjoy it any more. My mum wasn’t a big fan of me playing; she dressed me like a girly girl, with princess dresses and that kind of stuff, but I was never really like that at that age. I always wanted to follow my older brother – I wanted to wear his clothes. He started playing football before me and I wanted to be like him.”.

Industry observers note that baum would play on the side of the pitch at her brother’s club until a parent stated she should be playing too. After playing with various local teams she joined Hamburg’s academy. She worked her way into the first team and they won promotion to the second tier in her first season. In the 2024-25 season they reached the DFB-Pokal semi-finals and the top flight. Baum moved to RB Leipzig and scored five goals in 27 games before Arsenal swooped.

In a recent development, “Everything was just so quick,” she notes of the move to London. Training required getting used to: “Everything was so sharp, everything was technically excellent, like 10 out of 10. I was quite nervous and had some clumsy actions.”.

The transfer also involved swapping an average attendance last season of 1,651 for one of 33,808. “It’s unbelievable,” says Baum of playing at the Emirates Stadium. “I had only played in a big stadium once before. You can’t even believe how much the fans give you when you step on the pitch. There’s so much support, that of course we need in this current time. I think Arsenal is a club that holds on to us, on to the team, and gives us a lot of strength.”.

Look closely at Baum’s left wrist when she plays and you will usually see a strip of white tape around it. Sometimes it has something written on it. She’s done it “since that day” – the day in 2022 when Dennis died in a car accident, aged 17.

Industry observers note that the brother that inspired her on to a pitch is with her on it at the highest level. “The next time I was on the football pitch, I just felt I wanted to do that,” she notes. “I feel like it’s given me a different kind of strength and confidence. Sometimes I don’t write anything, but it’s about just having the physical feeling that he is with me.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ashleigh Neville joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer.
  • Charlton Athletic achieved the unthinkable last season when they earned promotion to the Women's Super League - but it has been a harsh introduction.
  • After 10 games in the top flight, Karen Hills' side are yet to pick up a point and have scored just five goals, conceding 30.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ashleigh Neville joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer.

Charlton Athletic achieved the unthinkable last season when they earned promotion to the Women's Super League - but it has been a harsh introduction.

After 10 games in the top flight, Karen Hills' side are yet to pick up a point and have scored just five goals, conceding 30.

They have already lost to the other promoted sides - Birmingham City and Crystal Palace - and are six points adrift at the bottom of the table.

The club expected a tough challenge as they made the jump up to the WSL for the first time but the results have still hit them hard.

"I'm trying everything I can," manager Hills noted following their 2-0 defeat by West Ham last weekend.

That result came a week after Charlton's 3-2 loss at Crystal Palace where they had been leading with 16 minutes to go.

So is it time to consider relegation, even in November, or is there still hope for Charlton to turn things around?

Charlton pipped better resourced teams in the WSL 2 last season, eventually beating top-flight side Leicester City in a play-off to secure promotion.

An incredible 27-game unbeaten run ended in March but was founded on an effective defensive structure and often heroics by goalkeeper Sophie Whitehouse.

However, the step up has proved difficult with inexperience and tight finances standing in the way.

Statistically, Charlton rank bottom in the WSL for average possession (30%), shots on target (17), passing accuracy (66%) and successful passes (1,689).

They have conceded nine times from set-pieces - the most in the WSL - and 14 of their total goals against have come in either the first or final 15 minutes in games.

In a recent development, the only other sides to lose their first 10 games in a WSL season are Doncaster Rovers Belles in 2016 and Yeovil Town in 2017-18. The Belles went on to win just one game as they were relegated, while Yeovil failed to win any, drawing two and finishing bottom, only avoiding relegation because of a league restructure.

Experienced defender Ashleigh Neville, who joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer, told BBC Sport: "We knew it was going to be a tough start to the season.

Industry observers note that "I was really excited to embrace that challenge. It's been difficult with results but when you look at the first game compared to now, I'd like to hope that people can see we're trying to build something.

"We're trying the hardest we can off the pitch to get to terms with how quick the game is compared to the WSL 2 and the quality of players we're up against.

"But it's still a joy to come into work and people are wanting to be better, asking how they can improve and move forward.".

This month, manager Hills insisted Charlton "will never throw the towel in" but admitted results are "hurting" the club.

Neville added: "It is not at the forefront of things but we've been really unlucky with the injuries that we've had in our attacking line.

"We're lacking in confidence going forward, and creativity for what we can actually provide.

It has been revealed that "It's a vicious circle. If you haven't got confidence because you're losing games, how do you still get that confidence in games where we need it the most?".

Whitehouse's penalty masterclass sends Charlton into WSL.

How WSL 2 title contenders Charlton are defying the odds.

Karen Hills was a player at Charlton Athletic before retiring in 2007.

Charlton are one of only three clubs without Premier League male counterparts to offer financial backing in the WSL and that restricts their freedom in recruitment.

It has not helped that summer signing Linda Lif Boama suffered a serious knee injury in September, defender Grace Johnston was ruled out in October and Paula Partido had to return to parent club London City Lionesses for knee surgery.

Charlotte Newsham, who played a key role in their WSL 2 promotion run, was also sidelined by an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury before the play-off victory.

While Charlton sought out shrewd signings in the summer, rivals Birmingham City were able to spend six-figure sums on Manchester United duo Lisa Naalsund and Millie Turner.

The Blues also broke their club record in January - a reported Â£316,000 fee for Wilma Leidhammar - while Oceane Hurtre was signed last summer to boost their second-tier title hopes and has now scored seven goals in 10 WSL games.

Fellow promoted club Palace picked up four-time WSL winner Bethany England and one of the WSL 2's standout players Lexi Lloyd-Smith in the summer.

"WSL 2 teams have to be even more ready for the WSL while they're still in the WSL 2 so that when they do make that jump, it's not a huge gap," noted Hills.

"The gap is continuing to get bigger and you see some of the players the top teams have brought in and the finances they have.

In a recent development, "It's a big challenge for us. We're finding that out on a weekly basis.".

Charlton benefited from the WSL's expansion this summer to 14 teams from 12 as organisers try to bridge the gap between the leagues and to increase the number of matches.

It was well-received by fans and those within the game, but Hills says it will still take time for WSL 2 clubs to catch up.

"If you look at the bottom three teams [in the table], it's all the newly-promoted teams. The level that we're coming into is already very well established.".

Neville added: "I think the financial side plays a massive part. We do our bit where we can. But it's hard to bring in the experienced players you need.".

Industry News: Kwame Brathwaite, photographer of 'Black is Beautiful' movement, dies at 85

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.
  • Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, announced his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

Brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in Upcoming York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

Using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

Sources indicate that “You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”.

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model.

Sources indicate that by the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

By the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands.

Throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The New Yorker.

T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is at the moment on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

Breaking: Earth is missing over a billion years of geological history. Scientists may have discovered why

💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than a billion years of Earth's history has seemingly vanished.
  • Across the planet, ancient rock formations contain colossal gaps in the geological record, leaving scientists puzzled over what happened to the missing chapters of our planet's past.
  • Now, researchers believe they may have found an explanation, and the answer lies deep inside Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than a billion years of Earth's history has seemingly vanished.

Across the planet, ancient rock formations contain colossal gaps in the geological record, leaving scientists puzzled over what happened to the missing chapters of our planet's past.

Now, researchers believe they may have found an explanation, and the answer lies deep inside Earth.

Industry observers note that normally, layers of sediment build up over time, eventually forming sedimentary rocks that preserve clues about our planet's past. Older layers generally lie beneath younger ones, allowing geologists to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

But the geological record isn't always so neatly arranged.

Industry observers note that one of the most striking examples is found in the Grand Canyon, where rocks separated by hundreds of millions of years sit directly on top of one another, as if some force or phenomenon removed the layers that geologists would expect to see in between. This enormous gap in Earth's geological timeline is part of the phenomenon known as the Great Unconformity.

It has been revealed that it's not just the Grand Canyon. Similar gaps have been identified across Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia. Depending on the location, the missing interval ranges from approximately 200 million years to more than a billion years.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out," study lead author Santosh Dhungana noted in a statement.

"The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance.".

In a new study published in the journal Nature, Dhungana and study co-author Nicolas Flament investigated whether activity far below Earth's surface was to blame.

Using computer models, they explored how the slow circulation of hot rock within Earth's mantle may have affected the continents over hundreds of millions of years.

The results suggest that three major ancient continental regions (Laurentia (modern North America), Baltica (northern Europe) and North China were gradually pushed up during the Neoproterozoic Era, approximately one billion to 540 million years ago. This would have left vast areas of land exposed to weathering and erosion for long periods, allowing water, wind and other processes to wear away rock that had formed much earlier.

But removing the rock is only part of the puzzle. They also needed to explain why the gaps are still visible today.

Their models suggest that the same regions subsequently began to sink. As sea levels rose relative to the land, sediment accumulated over the older, eroded surfaces, creating the sharp divide between ancient and younger rocks that we can still see today.

Crucially, the researchers found that the timing of the simulated continental uplift and sinking was consistent with geological evidence from North America, northern Europe and North China. This suggests that movements deep within Earth's mantle may have played a major role in shaping the geological record we see today.

She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

Now this is a revelation to wig out over.

Sarah Michelle Gellar and Freddie Prinze Jr.’s paths didn’t officially cross until the late ‘90s on I Know What You Did Last Summer, but as they recently learned they had more in common than they realized. Specifically, a shared family experience that traces back decades before they graced the screen.

“We always joke that the closest connection I had to my husband's side of the family,” Gellar told E! News in an exclusive interview, “was that for a small time I went to the same high school that my husband's dad went to, and that was like sort of our one thing.”.

Recent findings suggest that after all, though Gellar—mom to Charlotte, 17, and Rocky, 14, with Prinze—is a native Newly introduced Yorker, her husband was born in Los Angeles and grew up in New Mexico. (His dad Freddie Prinze, however, hailed from New York.).

In a recent development, she continued, “Then through Ancestry, we found out that our grandparents lived less than two miles away from each other in the Bronx at one point, which they could have potentially known each other. That's kind of crazy.”.

For the Buffy the Vampire Slayer star, who teamed up with Ancestry for its Gathering the Good initiative, it was an opportunity to explore her own family’s legacy while also looking at the spirit of giving through history. So, tracing how her loved ones made the journey to America in the 1890s at the same time philanthropist Lena Sittig space was creating what is now considered to be the modern toy drive, really hit home how interconnected the mission is.

“I learned that my grandmother was coming over on a ship at 16 years old, right when Lena was having her idea for this,” she shared. “It’s kind of crazy how the world intertwines, and it just reminds you that you're just such a small part of such a bigger picture.”.

It’s especially poignant as diving back into her roots has not always been a focal point for Gellar.

“It's funny, I didn't really spend that much time thinking about my history and my ancestry because I try so hard to live in the moment,” she explained. “And when Ancestry came to me and talked about what they wanted to do, I thought, ‘What a great idea to be able to learn acts of kindness, acts of goodness that your family may have been a part of that you never knew.’”.

As the Cruel Intentions alum knows, ‘tis the season to pay it forward. “The holiday season gets so dramatic—presents and all that,” she noted. “And I always look for what are the things that you could give someone that are really meaningful.”.

So, the 49-year-old posited, “What's more meaningful than learning about where you came from and your family and things you may not have known?”.

It has been revealed that to Gellar, it all comes back to Lena Sittig and her Brooklyn Christmas Tree Society, and how her idea is sparking change so many generations later. In fact, the Ringer actress teamed up with Ancestry to fulfill Christmas lists for Children’s Aid.

“So often, I think we think, ‘Well, I'm one person. What can I do?’ And then you see something like that, and you realize, oh wow, one person can do a lot,” she told E!. “But then to take it that step further, and maybe there's people in her family had no idea they were related to her.”.

Sources indicate that “Can you imagine going back in your history and finding out that one person in your family was responsible for millions of children's gifts all over the world because they had this idea?” Gellar added. “I think it's really special.”.

And it’s an experience Gellar wants to send far and wide, teasing what many of her loved ones—not to mention anyone looking to explore the impact their family has made on others—may be getting under the tree this year.

“There's something for me about the how tangible it was,” she admitted. “I saw signatures, I saw writing. it makes it seem just much more real to you than just getting an email that claims, ‘You know you came from here’ like, seeing their actual signatures at Ellis Island. It's also something too, growing up in Fresh York City, you forget about it. But this is the gateway.”.
