#82365. Brighton are rocking the Premier League elite. But can they mount a title tilt?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4219 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

Brighton are rocking the Premier League elite. But can they mount a title tilt?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4219 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A combination of smart analytics, a young manager and players hand-picked for their particular skills has the Seagulls flying high.
  • They lined up in sky‑blue shirts, white shorts.
  • But it was a Brighton midfielder who made the game’s first decisive contribution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A combination of smart analytics, a young manager and players hand-picked for their particular skills has the Seagulls flying high.

They lined up in sky‑blue shirts, white shorts. A combined value of £327m. Enzo Fernández, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Elliot Anderson were starting their first match together in Manchester City’s midfield.

But it was a Brighton midfielder who made the game’s first decisive contribution. Yasin Ayari slotted the ball home. The away crowd at the Etihad Stadium roared, then watched their team defend relentlessly, securing Brighton’s first league victory away to City.

In a recent development, it was 31 October 2026. There are dangers in reading too much into a single result this early in the season. Teams are still finding their rhythm, new signings bedding in. But this result packed some punch.

If spending decided football matches, Brighton & Hove Albion should not be competing with, let alone beating, Manchester City, who sign established stars for astronomical fees and wages. Erling Haaland is paid £525,000 a week.

According to an independent commission, to circumvent the Premier League’s spending limits, which restrict a club’s losses, City artificially inflated their commercial revenues by £830m between 2009 and 2018. Brighton, by contrast, tend to buy potential, scouring the market for undervalued talent, often in less prominent leagues. After developing them and benefiting from their performances, the club sell them for profits.

They paid just £3.5m for Ayari, offering him about £10,000 a week, and paired him in midfield with Chema Andrés and Pascal Gross, signed for a combined fee of less than £25m.

The most remarkable thing about Brighton’s win was that it wasn’t really a shock. In September, they dismantled Arsenal, the Premier League champions and favourites for the title. As they prepare for Sunday’s match at Hull, they are second in the league, sandwiched between Arsenal and City, and have scored more goals than anyone else in the division. How, then, do Brighton excel on the pitch without haemorrhaging money? And is there a ceiling to what they can achieve?

On a crisp late October morning, I drove to Brighton in search of answers. Deep inside the Amex, the club’s stadium, I met Paul Barber, Brighton’s CEO, a cheerful man who speaks with the calmness of someone with nowhere else to be.

“Being the size of club that we are, we had to find a way of being competitive that was probably different to any of the other bigger clubs that we were aiming to compete with,” Barber said, “because their revenues are always going to be higher: bigger stadiums, more established sponsorship models, bigger stars, bigger brands.”.

Hours before Brighton beat City, Chelsea had beaten Manchester United. In their respective midfields were Moisés Caicedo and Carlos Baleba, whom Brighton had signed for a combined fee of less than £30m and sold for about £180m. “It’s those trading profits that are effectively the core of the Brighton model,” Barber explained.

Recent findings suggest that most clubs recruit and develop talent, I pointed out, but few do it better than Brighton. Who, outside Ecuador, had heard of Caicedo before he signed for Brighton in 2021? Two years later, the world’s biggest clubs were competing for his signature. The same can be stated of dozens of others, among them Marc Cucurella and Alexis Mac Allister. One diamond exits, another enters. Caicedo replaced Yves Bissouma in central midfield. Baleba replaced Caicedo. The same applies to the dugout. Before joining Brighton, Fabian Hürzeler was coaching St Pauli in Germany; before him, Roberto De Zerbi had been at Shakhtar Donetsk.

Barber grinned. “There’s a myth that we have this secret supply of players,” he said. The explanation is Jamestown Analytics, a sports analytics organization founded by the club’s owner, Tony Bloom, as an offshoot of Starlizard, the gambling consultancy he established in 2006. Just as Starlizard uses proprietary modelling to identify mispriced odds in betting markets, Jamestown uses algorithms to identify underdeveloped football talents. “They’re all out there,” Barber said. “The data just enables Brighton to home in on them faster and earlier.”.

Sources indicate that when I asked for more detail about how the system works, Barber fiddled with his watch. Jamestown tracks a vast number of performance indicators for every player competing in professional football, many of which aren’t captured by other data providers. “Every action that players are taking on a football pitch is being looked at, measured and codified in some way,” he said.

According to recent reports, when the club identify a position to strengthen, they draw up a list of attributes for the ideal player. Some are universal to the position: a centre-back generally needs to be tall. Others depend on the specific coach and their style of football.

Recent findings suggest that later, when I spoke to Hürzeler, the head coach, he explained that the data had to reflect the specific demands of his playing system. “A player needs to have some basic things that fit our style of play, so if a player doesn’t want to have the ball then it’s difficult to play in our team. If a player doesn’t want to press high then it’s difficult to play in our team. These are just two examples.”.

One reason Brighton recruited Luka Vuskovic in July 2026 was because Hürzeler wanted a mobile centre-back. Reflecting on the City match, Barber recalled seeing Vuskovic pushing “so far forward that you’d have thought he was a right midfielder”. It was the sort of mobility Hürzeler’s system demanded, and Jamestown had identified.

Before Brighton’s victory over City, I met Mike Cave, the club’s sporting director, at the Lowry hotel in Manchester. A few of the Brighton players wandered around in club tracksuits. Cave wore a suit and tie and his hair was slicked back. He was telling me it was a big day without saying it.

Brighton’s recruitment advantage lies not simply in the quality and quantity of the data at their disposal, he said, but in their ability to interpret it and trust what it tells them. “You could have the best data in the world but if you’re not accustomed to using it, and if you’re not clear about how it informs your decision-making process, then it’s just a lot of data that doesn’t move the dial.”.

Recent findings suggest that the power of data is that it strips away emotions and preconceptions. When watching games, Hürzeler said he often identifies a player he thinks is performing well and texts Cave, only to learn that the numbers don’t support his impression. The conversation ends. “The numbers have to be right otherwise we have no chance of getting a player in.”.

Recent findings suggest that conversely, the data identifies players he might not otherwise have considered – such as Diego Gómez, the Paraguayan signed from Inter Miami in 2024. Despite the strength of Gómez’s underlying numbers, the club had a free run at signing him. Cave suggested this reflected a misconception that players in MLS aren’t equipped to play in the Premier League. “What the data has allowed us to do is step away from some of those biases and just be clear on what the evidence tells us, to look at the signal rather than the noise.”.

But identifying a player who can perform for Brighton is different from identifying one who will, Cave noted. The club’s requirements are so specific that the data typically identifies only around five candidates, Hürzeler says, and fewer still are affordable. Of those remaining, the recruitment team and Hürzeler will speak to anyone with experience of them – players, coaches and sponsors – to learn more about their character and personality, and prepare dossiers. Together, they’ll identify a primary target and make a move. “It’s not like I get a list and then decide which players; it’s something we all decide together,” said Hürzeler.

As Barber explained: “The more we can find out about a player’s character the less risk there is of that player being rejected like a bad organ transplant.” There’s no exhaustive list of desirable characteristics, he added, but “coachability” is key. Brighton’s model hinges on players having the capacity to improve, and the best indication is their drive to do so. “The biggest element of coachability is attitude.”.

Hürzeler asks himself: “What are they willing to give for their development? Are they willing to suffer?” He’s convinced this desire is innate. “These are things I can’t control.”.

Industry observers note that conversations with people around Gómez painted a picture of “a boy that is clearly trying to get absolutely everything out of his career”, noted Cave. But sometimes the qualities Brighton are looking for aren’t so obvious. Whereas the data is objective, indicates Barber, references are “someone’s opinion”. It’s challenging to know how much weight to give a single person’s negative judgment, particularly when it conflicts with other opinions, without dismissing it altogether. “Sometimes when you want to sign somebody you can subjectively screen out the negativity because you want them, and the data says you need them.”.

Beyond character, the team consider a player’s ability to settle into a new country, and whether their partner will, too. Once Brighton make an offer, the player is normally keen to join, in Barber’s experience, because they know it can lead to a move to “potentially bigger things”. The selling club is often receptive because there are rarely any other comparable offers on the table.

But this has been changing, says Barber. Brighton’s success means their interest in a player “alerts other clubs to that talent”, creating competition. Selling clubs, meanwhile, have reason to believe that the player “has the potential to be valued for a lot more”. Increasingly, then, Brighton are having to pay more, making “our ability to trade profitably ever harder”.

Sources indicate that even if a deal can be agreed, it doesn’t always represent good business. As Cave explained: “You’re dealing with human beings, in a complex system and a complex game, so you will never have a 100% strike record.”.

Asked what Brighton looks for in recruits, Gordon Greer, who played for the club from 2010 to 2016, was quick to answer: “high potential”. But that potential rarely means they’re ready to slot into the first‑team. Today, as Brighton’s pathway development manager, Greer’s job is to bridge that gap.

To understand how Greer does this, I joined him for coffee at the Lowry. He told me that he begins planning a player’s development while the club are still negotiating his signing. “In the buildup to us signing him, we’ll start to analyse him … what’s his strengths, what’s his weaknesses … where do we think we can help?” Once he’s met the player and understood their ambitions, he turns that assessment into a development initiative.

It has been revealed that to begin, Greer explained, he asked himself: “What are this player’s limiting factors to play for Brighton?” Sometimes the answer lies off the pitch. Hürzeler requires his players to speak English. It helps embed his playing principles by allowing the players to transmit them to each other. “We want to have a common language, so they can coach each other on the pitch,” he explained. Other times the shortcomings are more directly related to football, such as back‑post defending. A typical one is physicality; Hürzeler’s counter-pressing requires repeated sprints and many recruits would risk injury if they were thrown into the first team. “The game is so fast, and the intensity is crazy,” Jack Hinshelwood, who made his first‑team debut in 2023, has mentioned.

One pathway for development is the under-21s team, Greer says, but the physical demands of the game fall short of those in the Premier League. Hinshelwood, who came through the under-21s, suffered a stress fracture in his foot after a few top-flight games. “You need time to adapt,” he noted. In Greer’s view, the level doesn’t challenge most recruits enough for them to learn. “We want to put them in a position where they’re stretched enough that they’re uncomfortable but they’ve got enough success that they’re doing things that they enjoy.”.

An alternative is the loan market. Since 2018–19, Brighton have agreed more than 20 loan deals in each campaign. Playing time is an important consideration when arranging a loan, Greer explains, because a player’s value can drop if they’re not playing often. But he also considers the location, manager, formation and quality of the pitch. Position is crucial, too. Sending a striker to a team near the bottom of their league, where they’re likely to be living off scraps, can see their confidence and value drop, but sending a defender into the same environment can accelerate their development with repeated defensive situations. “You’re trying to get to a point where they’re impacting the game.”.

Recent findings suggest that A successful loan addresses a player’s limitations. “You’re trying to expose someone to something totally different,” Greer added. In 2017, Ben White – now of Arsenal and England – was loaned to Newport County to improve the “urgency in his defending”.

According to recent reports, “The game model was end‑to-end, back-to-front, League Two, where you’re up against it,” Greer added. In 2024, Ibrahim Osman, shortly after signing from Nordsjælland in Denmark, went to Feyenoord, a possession-based team, to develop his technical game. “Physically, he was a beast, but he was quite untidy,” mentioned Greer.

According to recent reports, throughout a loan, each player is continually reassessed. Those ready are brought into Hürzeler’s first team. If they’re not, another spell elsewhere might be arranged. But if their development has stalled for too long, they’ll be encouraged to leave permanently. That was the case with Leo Østigård, a Norway international signed from Molde in 2018. He was a skilled defender but he “wasn’t good enough on the ball”, Greer noted. His development slowed down during a loan at Coventry, and then, at Stoke, it became “clear he wasn’t going to be for us”.

Rather than continuing to work on Østigård’s weaknesses, the club sought to maximise his strengths. A loan was arranged at Genoa, a defensive team where Østigård would shine. A year later, he signed for Napoli. “We tried everything but it didn’t work,” Greer said, “so we thought: ‘How do we create as much value as possible?’”.

After speaking to Barber, I headed to Brighton’s training base, a short drive away from the Amex, to meet Hürzeler. Academy players milled around outside, while the first team was elsewhere preparing to face Getafe in the Conference League, a competition Brighton are being tipped to win.

I noticed a mural bearing the words: “Challenge the Establishment,” a reference to the so-called substantial six clubs. A member of staff pointed out that the mural had been Hürzeler’s idea, but the philosophy it exhibits has existed since Bloom took over the club in 2009. Brighton, the member of staff whispered to me, saw themselves as the “antidote” to big-spending clubs such as City.

In a recent development, before Hürzeler and I sat down in the press conference room, another journalist asked him whether he thought Brighton could win the title. He dismissed the question. His focus was improving the team, he mentioned. He suggested to me, however, that victories such as that over City were the fruits of his work developing the squad and an environment that allows talents to excel. “If you work with players for a longer time, you get used to each other and they get more and more of your principles.”.

According to recent reports, hürzeler tells me he relies on older players who embody these principles, such as Lewis Dunk and Pascal Gross. At 33, Hürzeler is younger than both, and became the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history when he was appointed in 2024. When you’re developing raw talents from abroad, while constantly selling and bringing in new players, you need a core group to “build the right culture”. Hinshelwood told me he has experienced this first-hand: “I remember watching their habits every day, how they live their lives, how they’re training, what they’re doing in the gym, how they’re communicating, and I learned so much just by watching them.”.

Hürzeler also emphasised the importance of tailoring the support players receive. “You can’t treat a player like Yankuba Minteh who is coming from [the] Gambia the same as a player like Lewis Dunk, who comes from England,” he remarked. He wants to cultivate an environment in which, as he put it, players, “no matter which age, no matter from where they are coming from, can express themselves”.

According to recent reports, to that end, Hürzeler appointed Mike Anthony, who spent 14 years working with New Zealand Rugby, as head of player development and high performance – a new role. One of Anthony’s priorities, he said, has been giving the players more responsibility. Players and the coaches increasingly “lead the programme together”, with players invited to lead discussions.

“They don’t want to just execute things, they want to be valued, they want to be appreciated, they want to be heard by us coaches,” Hürzeler noted. “If you don’t give them ownership and responsibility off the pitch, how can you expect them to take responsibility for their own execution on the pitch? It’s not possible.”.

It has been revealed that A key part of his role, Hürzeler told me, is listening to his players. It helps them perform, and makes him a better coach. He was reminded of this in February 2025, when there were calls for him to lose his job after a poor run that included a 7-0 defeat at Nottingham Forest. James Milner and Danny Welbeck suggested he was overcomplicating his messaging around counter-pressing. Taking their advice on board, he made changes that helped turn things around. “It was definitely one reason why we turned around the results.”.

Asked why Brighton have such a strong record for developing talent, Hinshelwood smiled: “You’re allowed to make mistakes, not effort mistakes, or applying yourself badly, but if you make a technical mistake you know you’ve got 10 other players who want you to try things,” he stated.

In a recent development, hürzeler also credited the club’s summer recruitment with this season’s success. Yet Brighton had sold Jan Paul van Hecke to Tottenham and Baleba to United, I pointed out. How could a club expect to improve while selling their best players?

Although he often tries to prevent departures by convincing Bloom not to sell, Hürzeler said he has no final say. “I can’t control whether a player gets a substantial offer and Tony wants to accept this offer.” But he’s come to see departures as an opportunity to revitalise the squad with upcoming profiles. “When you sign for Brighton, you know that it’s part of the identity, so automatically you have the mindset that you have to deal with these things.”.

According to recent reports, being transparent about the club’s model with coaches is a crucial component in their success, according to Barber, but even then it can create tensions. The decision to sell Caicedo was one reason De Zerbi departed, as was the Italian’s insistence on massive-name signings rather than trusting the data. It’s no different with supporters, Barber said: “Sometimes when a big player leaves a club and the fans are blindsided by that, it creates this bigger sense of injustice, anger, disappointment.”.

Industry observers note that barber also explains that he must go to great lengths to keep costs down. “The difference between what we bring in and what we spend is what we put out on the pitch.” The club’s use of experienced players such as Dunk is ultimately driven by financial constraints. They can’t afford to sign players in their prime, either in transfer fees or wages, so rely on players a little past their prime to counterbalance the inexperience of their younger recruits. “They’re providing that level of experience of a 27-, 28-, 29-year-old, albeit four or five years later, but at a much lower cost.”.

It has been revealed that brighton also use data to identify and recruit coaches whose philosophy aligns with the existing squad, minimising the need to overhaul the squad to fit a upcoming style of football. Hürzeler was identified in large part because the numbers showed he could build on the players he inherited. “Revolutions cost a lot of money,” Barber remarked. “If you can match the coach that you’re bringing into the squad that you’ve got, the cost of change is minimal.”.

Recent findings suggest that the final part of the model is knowing when to sell. Barber tries to have a replacement through the door before letting a player go. It becomes trickier to negotiate a fee for a replacement when the selling club knows Brighton have just sold a player for £100m. Barber told me he delayed selling Caicedo until he was confident Baleba could step up. “We felt Carlos had a lot of potential that we could help to realise quite swiftly … he’s a quick learner and quite raw, but at the same time you could see rapid improvements in him.”.

Recent findings suggest that but other factors matter too, such as whether a player still has room to develop, and therefore increase his value further; the state of the market; and the risk that turning down an offer might jeopardise the chance of a future sale. “If there is a dearth of central midfielders at the moment, maybe now is the time to sell because there will be a significant premium because there are no other options.”.

According to recent reports, barber adds that refusing to sell Caicedo to Arsenal in January 2023 was easier because other clubs wanted him in the summer. “Not doing the deal didn’t affect our ability to do the deal with Liverpool and then Chelsea the following summer.”.

In their last match before the November international break, Brighton beat Brentford and leapfrogged City. They’d progressed in Europe too: a goal from Malick Yalcouyé, a £6m signing from ​​IFK Göteborg, had beaten Getafe. Outside the ground, fans were dreaming of titles. Barber said he hoped they would not have to wait much longer. “We now need to take the next step and put some silverware on the table.”.

Recent findings suggest that but if Brighton are to compete for major trophies, I wondered, will they have to invest more heavily in players, and keep them in their prime? Can the club’s current model allow them to become part of the establishment, rather than simply challenging it?

The club are already adapting, says Barber. The signing of Vuskovic for a club record £46m demonstrates an appetite for talents better equipped to immediately contribute to the first team. “Those players are already at a level of transfer fee that we wouldn’t have contemplated, and 10 years ago we wouldn’t have even considered.” As Jamestown’s algorithm improves, Barber says, he’s hopeful it will become easier for the club to invest these sorts of sums in players, because the risk of getting the assessment wrong will be lower.

Industry observers note that but Barber believes player trading is likely to stay as the core of the club’s strategy, partly because they are good at it, but also because they need the revenue. “There’s always going to be this gap [in commercial sales and ticket revenue] so the need for us to trade will always be there.” Even if they did decide to keep players such as Baleba and Van Hecke, would they be able to? As much as a title or two might make it easier to convince top players to stay, Barber mentioned he struggles to envisage a time when they’ll be able to compete with the bigger clubs on wages.

And even if Brighton could one day afford to retain their best players, would it make them less attractive to the next generation of recruits, who might no longer see the club as a stepping stone on the way to the so-called establishment? Could the club become so successful that the prices of their targets rise beyond what they can afford? Might the model self-cannibalise?

It has been revealed that hürzeler tells me he reflects on these same questions. “It’s interesting, this discussion, because these kinds of discussions we also have in the building.” When we spoke on the phone before the Hull match, I brought up Hearts, who have partnered with Jamestown and came close to winning the Scottish title in May for the first time since 1960, challenging the Celtic-Rangers duopoly. I asked whether this gave him the belief that Brighton could go one step further and break the massive clubs’ stranglehold.

“Of course, you see this as motivation for what is possible,” he noted. He revealed a belief that he can lift a trophy with Brighton, which is why he has extended his contract to 2029. “When I see the team now, they are so into it, they are so committed to it.” He just wouldn’t say when. “Will it be this season? I don’t know. Will it be next season? I don’t know.” Beyond that, he tries not to give it much attention. “These kinds of questions, we can answer them one day.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hearts are now the highest scorers in the Premiership with 34 goals from 13 games.

Watch Dundee v Hearts highlights.

"I've been in football 37 years and I've never experienced anything like that," noted a hugely dispirited Steven Pressley after Dundee were demolished 8-0 at home by Hearts on Saturday.

The jubilant victors can top that span of time by quite a distance given they are celebrating their biggest away win since they began playing league football in the 1890s, a result which also happens to be Dundee's record home defeat.

It was just the third 8-0 game in Scottish top-flight history, after Rangers crushed Clyde in 1931 and Celtic hammered Hamilton in 1988.

The eight at Dens Park came from 14 efforts on target and an expected goals (xG) of just 3.5.

Ruthless Hearts put eight past ramshackle 10-man Dundee.

There were some fine finishes, a deft first-time effort from Sabah Kerjota being the pick of the bunch, a lot of shoddy defending, and a red card for the hosts before the hour with the score at 4-0.

Just the tonic for Hearts after three defeats in a week prior to the international break, including a League Cup semi-final derby and a shellacking from Falkirk which ended their 19-month unbeaten league streak at Tynecastle.

It has been revealed that "They really looked like a team again," enthused former club hero John Robertson on Sportsound. "The rotations were good, the passing was good. The guys coming off the bench wanted to be part of this and they just kept going and going.".

Another ex-Hearts player, Michael Stewart, called it the "perfect evening".

"To come here and win was the most crucial thing, but to do it in such a fashion is as good a reset as you're ever going to get," he said on Premier Sports.

Hearts are the Premiership's top scorers with 34 from 13 outings.

Add goals against and you have a whopping tally of 56, with five conceded at home to Falkirk last time and seven shipped at Celtic Park last month.

This was just a third league blank for Wouter Vrancken's defence.

"It sounds crazy after scoring eight, but the clean sheet is maybe the most crucial thing," added Robertson. "They just haven't had enough of them.".

Reflecting on the biggest win of his career, the Belgian appeared to agree, telling BBC Sport Scotland: "What actually pleased me the most was at six or seven when Dundee were countering, nine players were sprinting back to fight for a clean sheet.

"These are the things we want to see.".

Vrancken on Hearts' demolition of Dundee.

Hearts returned from the previous international break with a 5-0 win over St Mirren before the heavy loss to Celtic and Vrancken is certainly not getting carried away with nine more games coming over the next 30 days, beginning at home to Monaco in the Conference League on Thursday.

"We had talks before our days off, they were really honest and open," he revealed.

"It was good to hear but you have to take ownership of it on the pitch. You can talk as much as you want but if you can't show it on the pitch it doesn't mean anything.

According to recent reports, "When you do it like this it's the first step. But it's only the first step, only one game and we have to try to bring more.

"It was ruthless but the schedule is also ruthless â but we got a good boost from tonight.".

Having gone into the international break on the back off those three successive losses, Hearts fans may have been apprehensive.

After all, Dundee had lost just once at Dens Park all season, back in August.

However, the hosts were abject, allowing Hearts so much room.

"Every aspect of our performance was below par," bemoaned Pressley. "We looked unmotivated and lacking edge.

Pressley says 8-0 defeat is 'on him'.

"Of course the sending off made the second half very difficult, but we didn't do the things that are normally associated with our performance.

"We weren't gritty enough in our defending, we didn't fill the spaces we normally do. We normally defend in a particularly strong manner, but we didn't do that.

It has been revealed that "I can only apologise. My thoughts are that it's on myself. It's my responsibility to make sure you see a motivated Dundee team, it is my responsibility to make sure we are tactically sound, it is my responsibility to make sure they show grit and determination and not go under like we did.

"I had a little sense we haven't been quite on it over the last couple of weeks but I never expected that and I take ownership.".

On this day in space! Nov. 18, 2013: NASA launches MAVEN spacecraft to Mars to find out how the Red Planet lost its water

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars.
  • Recent findings suggest that the name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN.
  • MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars.

Recent findings suggest that the name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN. The spacecraft was an orbiter designed to help scientists figure out what happened to the water on Mars and its atmosphere. Mars is dry today, but it data from several Mars missions suggest that it was a much wetter environment a long time ago.

MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars. The planet has a super thin atmosphere that has been leaking into space for a few billion years. Scientists think that when Mars lost its atmosphere, water dried up on the surface as a result.

Industry observers note that solar storms that blast radiation into the solar system appear to have blasted away some of the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere once kept Mars warm enough to sustain liquid water on its surface, and losing that greenhouse gas turned Mars into a cold and dry place.

NASA's MAVEN spacecraft was the first Mars orbiter ever built to measure how the Martian atmosphere interacts with solar wind, as well as how that constant stream of particles from the sun slowly stripped the Red Planet of its precious atmosphere over time.

In a recent development, after its launch in 2013, MAVEN spent about 10 months en route to Mars before entering orbit on Sept. 21, 2014. The spacecraft then spent the better part of 11 years studying the Red Planet from orbit using three different suites of instruments: An imaging ultraviolet spectrograph to study the global characteristics of the Martian atmosphere; a Neutral Gas and Ion Mass Spectromenter to measure its composition; and a six-instrument setup to study how Mars' ionosphere reacts to solar wind.

"The science MAVEN has given us is key to informing what kind of radiation protection and safety measures we must take before sending humans to Mars," Louise Prockter, NASA director of planetary science, said in June 2026 after the mission concluded. "The data collected from MAVEN will continue to provide valuable insight into Mars for decades to come.".

Industry observers note that MAVEN was originally designed to study Mars for 1 full Earth year after arriving at the Red Planet. That mission ended in 2016, but the spacecraft managed to survive for another 10 years adding more observations for scientists to study.

In a recent development, NASA ultimately began using MAVEN as a communications relay for other missions at Mars as the orbiter aged. In December 2025, MAVEN went silent, with NASA losing communication with the orbiter.

An investigation later found that the probe sent its final signal on Dec. 6, 2025 as it was heading behind Mars (as seen from Earth). But when it emerged on the other side, it had gone into an uncontrollable spin that led to a loss of power, dooming the spacecraft.

NASA tried in vain to recover the spacecraft over several months, ultimately declaring the mission over in June 2026.

In a recent development, "Best. Mars. Mission. Ever," Shannon Curry, MAVEN's principal investigator, said of the probe's entire 12.5-year mission when it ended. The team "really experienced the loss of a loved one with the end of the mission here.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial-intelligence tools are helping citizen scientists to find undiscovered exoplanets (artist’s illustration).Credit: Hypersphere/SPL.
  • In a recent development, in September, Pavel Rabtsevich sat down at his computer and asked an AI model to discover a planet.
  • History’s long-secret codes are being cracked by amateurs using AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial-intelligence tools are helping citizen scientists to find undiscovered exoplanets (artist’s illustration).Credit: Hypersphere/SPL.

In a recent development, in September, Pavel Rabtsevich sat down at his computer and asked an AI model to discover a planet. Rabtsevich directed the bot to a specific batch of telescope data and gave it a high-level plan to hunt for evidence of undetected planets. In about two weeks, the bot delivered the goods: two possible planets orbiting a star 116 light years from Earth. Professional astronomers are now checking the bot’s findings.

History’s long-secret codes are being cracked by amateurs using AI.

History’s long-secret codes are being cracked by amateurs using AI.

Rabtsevich, who works in Spain as an artificial-intelligence specialist and has no formal astronomy education, is one of the most successful of a wave of amateur astronomers who are using AI models to search for worlds outside the Solar System. Citizen scientists have been using publicly available tools from NASA and other researchers to find planets for decades. But AI’s ability to scour the internet for such tools and use them to process massive amounts of data has lowered the barrier to entry for non-specialists who want to become planet hunters.

The newfound accessibility of data-analysis tools, however, has meant that not all amateurs are doing research responsibly, says Michelle Kunimoto, an exoplanet researcher at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, Canada. Some planet hunters don’t fully understand the algorithms being used by AI tools and thus can’t validate the models’ findings, Kunimoto says. “There’s been a huge, overwhelming surge of AI-driven papers, which tend to have [planet] candidates that are not the best quality,” they say. And as a result, “the systems we use to disseminate science are being overwhelmed”.

Recent findings suggest that for his search, Rabtsevich enlisted Claude Code, an AI coding tool made by Anthropic. He asked it to sift through data from more than 120,000 stars observed by NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) in late 2025 and early 2026. He guided Claude to use a popular planet-detection algorithm to search for dips in the stars’ brightness. A regular and repeated dimming of a star can be a sign that a planet is orbiting it and blocking a little bit of light every time it passes between the star and an observer.

Claude zeroed in on a star called TIC 4206066 that demonstrated two separate cycles of dimming, one roughly every 3 days and another every 11 days. That suggests that TIC 4206066 is orbited by two planets, one of which loops around the star more tightly than the other and thus takes less time to complete a full rotation.

These alien planets are astronomers’ favourites.

These alien planets are astronomers’ favourites.

Sources indicate that rabtsevich instructed Claude to look for those same repetitive patterns in archival TESS data. Sure enough, data from 2018 and 2020 recorded the same pattern of dimming coming from TIC 4206066. At Rabtsevich's direction, Claude then found a planet-detection algorithm, one written and made publicly available by Kunimoto, and ran it to validate the signals.

Rabtsevich published his findings to the platform Zenodo as a preprint1 on 25 September. His work has not been peer reviewed, but TESS astronomers have completed an independent analysis of the signals and have added them to their official list of planet candidates.

Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.
  • About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
  • Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC claims.

Cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the Newly introduced York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC claims the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

According to recent reports, lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A new study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

The researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort.

According to recent reports, as lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s crucial to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

Further study is required, stated study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

It has been revealed that “Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz remarked in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

Recent findings suggest that the implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

“If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”.

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic.

Dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

It has been revealed that “It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the fresh research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”.

Recent findings suggest that other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

In a recent development, A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer stated. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

It has been revealed that “There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer remarked. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”.

Who are you and what is your job role?

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

According to recent reports, becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and stated sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your proposal and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

In a recent development, with a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

Recent findings suggest that if you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:.

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees fresh referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she claims. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared.".

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she notes. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that manchester City are living in Premier League purgatory, without a win in four, but at least against Fulham they ended a three-game losing run. As they await their fate after being found guilty of financial breaches, their form has slumped. This passive draw was met with boos from the home fans.

Arguments will be made over Erling Haaland’s disallowed goal but City did not deserve anything more. The Norwegian uncharacteristically missed a number of fine chances as Rodrigo Muniz took advantage of City’s porous defence. They had to rely on Elliot Anderson to get anything out of the fixture.

It is the first time Fulham have avoided defeat against City in 21 attempts going back to 2011, while City have conceded in nine consecutive games for the first time since 2019. Enzo Maresca and his side’s problems go beyond legal wrangling.

City approached the game in the same subdued manner of the crowd, as is customary for a Saturday lunchtime kick-off. They offered little in the way of dynamism from the off. A couple of half chances were brushed off by Fulham, who were allowed to ease themselves into the game as slow-starters City conceded the opener for a fourth straight match.

Confusion between defence and midfield has repeatedly caused problems under Maresca, who saw Marc Guéhi cross the halfway line to press a throw-in deep inside the Fulham half. When the visitors won the first header, the centre-back was out of position and everything was far too simple from then on.

In the 16th ​minute, Oscar Bobb, a former City winger, shimmied and Muniz curled his shot into the top corner from the edge of the box.

Recent findings suggest that city finally found intent midway through the first half. Iliman Ndiaye’s dangerous cross found Haaland at the back post but he could not finish, allowing Bernd Leno to get his hands to the ball but whether the German had it under control is another matter. Haaland jabbed at the goalkeeper, nudging the ball through his grasp. Thomas Bramall and the video assistant referee gave the keeper the benefit of the doubt. Leno later told BBC Sport: “I had the feeling I controlled the ball and Haaland crashed into me and slid into me. It was a wet pitch. I was hoping VAR doesn’t overturn it. For me it was a foul.”.

• Fulham avoided defeat against Manchester City for the first time since September 2011 in all competitions, ending the longest ever winning streak one team has had against another in English football (20 matches).

• Manchester City have conceded in nine consecutive games in all competitions for the first time since a run to December 2019 (10), while they have conceded the opening goal in four consecutive Premier League games for the first time since a run to April 2012 (5).

• Manchester City have trailed at half-time in four consecutive Premier League games for only the third time, after October 1995 and April 2006. Opta.

According to recent reports, maresca disagreed. “From my point of view, it’s quite clear that it’s not foul but I’m not the guy that decides, unfortunately,” he said.

According to recent reports, city lacked a cutting edge. Phil Foden, given the nod over Rayan Cherki at No 10, could not get on the same wavelength as the misfiring Haaland, whose clinical finishing deserted him.

City continued to find it difficult as David Affengruber and Calvin Bassey put in fine performances at centre-back, snuffing out every danger. To find a way back, City needed to increase the tempo and Anderson obliged by volleying a cleared corner into the bottom corner from 18 yards.

In an underperforming team lacking energy, the England international is a catalyst. He latched on to a Haaland flick-on but could not stay on his feet. The pair combined for a second time only for Anderson’s quick feet and cute finish to end with the ball slipping an inch wide in the 65th minute, City’s last meaningful opportunity.

As the game ebbed to a close, City’s flaws were exposed as Fulham won the ball and Muniz was through on goal. Gianluigi Donnarumma was the last – and sturdiest – line of defence, repeating the feat against Bassey soon after as Fulham continued to look sharp and City blunt.

The jeers at the end stated it all.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

According to recent reports, I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Industry observers note that growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

In a recent development, so a typical day for us, we'll get a upcoming build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save.".

Recent findings suggest that so as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

So I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a new job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

One of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

Working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.

Sources indicate that CJ works as an associate quality assurance manager on the video game Football Manager. His team test the game to make sure everything works, and collaborate with the developers to create the most realistic simulation of football.

There are lots of different ways to progress in the gaming industry.

Recent findings suggest that CJ works in the QA (Quality Assurance) team, testing games. In this team, his career progression has followed this path:.

QA tester --> QA lead --> QA manager.

His team is just one of the options, though. "There are lots of other roles within the industry too, including production, game design, social media and development, where developers help to code the game," he explains. "Depending on your skills and interests, there are different pathways you can take that you might enjoy and be suited to.".

There are different roles in video game testing. CJ notes that: "Salaries can vary depending on your role and the company you work for. They can range from around Â£20,000 to Â£50,000 and upwards." The higher salaries in this range could apply when you've gained more experienced and progressed in your career.

CJ is now a quality assurance manager, but he started out as a quality assurance tester. Find out more about the role of QA tester below. This role can have various other job titles, such as games tester, computer games tester, and video games tester.

You could get into this role via a university course, a college course (such as a Level 3 Diploma in Creative Media, an A-level in Computing, or a T-level in Digital Software Development (England only)), an apprenticeship, or applying directly if you have relevant experience.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that not since the emergence of a certain Harry Kane has there been this much excitement about a player from Tottenham’s academy. On his first senior start, Luca Williams-Barnett demonstrated just why as the 18-year-old became their youngest Premier League goalscorer since Gareth Bale in 2007 before teeing up Dominic Solanke with a mesmerising and match-winning assist against Ipswich.

According to recent reports, that made it four league victories from their last five matches for Roberto De Zerbi’s side and the Italian could only have enjoyed the view from the stands as he served his one-match touchline ban. Tottenham have struggled to match their London rivals Arsenal and Chelsea’s record of producing homegrown players in recent years but they appear to have struck gold with Williams-Barnett.

Sources indicate that harry Winks was the last academy graduate to score on his debut more than a decade ago – a feat that Kane also achieved two years earlier against Sunderland. Yet after Spurs decided to allow the England Under-21s striker Will Lankshear to join Middlesbrough in the summer, there was no chance that Williams-Barnett would be allowed to follow him out of the door. He became the 900th player ever to represent Spurs when he made his debut last year and the teenager left the field here to a standing ovation that he will never forget.

It has been revealed that “I told him to play like he plays in the park with his friends, with the same freedom,” remarked De Zerbi. “And to play and to work hard without the ball, like [Ousmane] Dembélé, like Raphinha, like [Lamine] Yamal. Luca is a special player. I’m not surprised because his talent is bigger than you think. He’s very young but at same time he’s very mature. He is older than his age.”.

Asked whether his protege has the potential to be compared to the Barcelona sensation Lamine Yamal, De Zerbi added: “Yes, I think so. One of the best things in my career I’ve seen today on the bus to the stadium. He was watching [clips] on YouTube of Ronaldinho, Hazard. I think he’s a special guy, because if one hour before you are debuting in the Premier League, you are watching Ronaldinho, Hazard, Neymar, all these types of talent. Having the qualities is one thing but he has the passion for football, too.”.

After a promising start to the campaign, Ipswich’s momentum has stalled – they have now gone five games without a victory. But Gary O’Neil, who has already seen 16-year-old Max Dowman score twice for Arsenal against his side in the Carabao Cup, acknowledged that they had been second best throughout. “You need things to be perfect when we come to a place like this and we didn’t make things easy for ourselves,” he stated.

Recent findings suggest that de Zerbi dropped a huge hint that Williams-Barnett could be handed his opportunity to start after two impressive cameos against Crystal Palace and Leeds. “Maybe, maybe,” he said on Friday. It turned out that the decision was actually taken last week, although the absence of Sandro Tonali due to illness forced Spurs into a reshuffle in midfield as Mateus Fernandes was handed the holding role.

According to recent reports, solanke has struggled to fill the void left by Kane since joining from Bournemouth in 2024 but looked in determined mood and he was inches wide with a swivel and shot from inside the area. A driving run from Williams-Barnett had the home supporters off their feet, with Solanke again going close from the resulting corner. It then needed a timely block from the teenager to stop Ipswich breaking downfield.

His massive moment arrived less than 60 seconds later. Porro’s ball to the back post should have been dealt with by Abdoul Ouattara, only for a moment’s hesitation to allow Williams-Barnett to muscle in front of him and apply the finish with his knee. “He’s one of our own,” sang the Tottenham fans in delight.

It has been revealed that mohammed Kudus was unfortunate to see his superb effort from a free-kick cannon off the inside of the post and away to safety. Williams-Barnett will be disappointed not to have scored his second when he miskicked inside the six-yard box with the goal gaping. James Maddison was then denied by a brilliant save from Christian Walton and Williams-Barnett left the field at half-time looking very pleased with himself as he waved to his family in the crowd.

His smile grew even broader after Darnell Furlong was left bamboozled by a direct run down the left flank before the youngster delivered the ball on a plate for Solanke to score his first goal here since March. The defeat could have been worse for Ipswich had it not been for Walton, and O’Neil will know they are in danger of being sucked into trouble if this winless run continues. There are no such concerns for Tottenham these days. Thanks to Williams-Barnett, their future looks much brighter than a few weeks ago.

Nguyen Quynh Anh's reign as Miss Universe Vietnam has officially come to an end.

The beauty queen was initially suspended in October when private messages speaking negatively about other pageant participants became public, and now the organizers have revoked her title due to Nguyen's conduct while under suspension.

In a recent development, the challenges occurred while Nguyen was barred from performing in all "artistic performance activities" related to Miss Universe for six months, the show’s organizers, Five6 Entertainment, announced in a Nov. 18 statement, according to Tuoi Tre News.

In addition to being suspended from events for the group text—which included runner-up Trinh My Anh—containing derogatory remarks about past winners, fellow contestants and judges, the model was ordered to pay a fine, the outlet noted.

However, when the influencer attended a community event while banned from representing the pageant, the production company, per Tuoi Tre News, remarked her appearance caused challenges that "affected the image of Miss Universe Vietnam and its organizers.".

In addition to promoting her title while suspended, the organizers stated that the 27-year-old delayed signing her management contract in order to prioritize a "mental health condition" amid the transitional period. Still, the team said they learned Nguyen signed an exclusive contract with a competitor management agency and "continued accepting performance engagements and attending events without reaching an agreement with Five6.".

In response to the initial backlash, the competition's runner-up, Trinh, apologized on Instagram. Meanwhile, Nguyen released an Oct. 13 statement transcribed by the outlet where she apologized "to the women concerned and everyone affected by this incident, especially the audience.".

Sources indicate that "I understand that holding a beauty queen title does not make me incapable of making mistakes," her statement continued. "However, the title requires me to be more mindful and careful about my words, conduct and responsibilities, even in seemingly minor matters.".

E! News has reached out to Nguyen Quynh Anh regarding the recent conduct allegations but has not yet heard back.

The release noted that her title was formally revoked after reviewing the conditions of holding the crown, the outlet stated.

And given the unexpected exit, Vietnam will not send a competitor to the global Miss Universe finale on Nov. 24 in Puerto Rico.

Latest Update: Astronomers witness a star eating its companion in 1st-of-its-kind observation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (630 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a fresh study reports.
  • As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby.
  • "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in New York, told Space.com.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a fresh study reports.

As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now.

"Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in New York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean. We need sensitive telescopes monitoring the sky for a long time in order to catch this effect.".

It has been revealed that in the new study, the researchers investigated a red giant star designated WNTR23bzdiq, which is located about 2.5 million light-years away in the Andromeda galaxy. The star is about seven times heftier and 350 times wider than our own sun.

Industry observers note that in 2023, using NASA's now-defunct NEOWISE space telescope and the WINTER telescope at Palomar Observatory in California, the scientists noticed that this star was brightening. By analyzing previous records, they found that the red giant had gradually started growing more luminous in 2018.

The researchers had previously suggested this brightening potentially occurred because the giant star engulfed a companion star. As this companion spiraled toward the giant's core, it would generate friction, heat and light, explaining the increasing luminosity.

According to recent reports, then, near the end of 2025, the astronomers saw a giant eruption of light from this giant star. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope observed the star just 47 days after that eruption, allowing the team to characterize the event in detail. The researchers now propose that this explosion happened when a companion star about 70% the sun's mass rammed into the giant's heart.

"I was absolutely flabbergasted when we saw this," Karambelkar said.

Recent findings suggest that in the fresh study, the scientists estimated that the eruption expelled an amount of material equal to about 0.1 to 0.2 times the mass of the sun. "Stars engulfing their companions have been theorized for many decades, and this event provides the first observations of this theoretical prediction," Karambelkar said.

Although these findings suggest that two stars — a binary system nicknamed "Bao" — merged into one, "it is not the only possibility," Karambelkar stated. "The other possibility is that both stars survived, in a much shorter orbit. In order to conclusively determine what happened, we need to continue monitoring what the system does, once the heft of the eruption settles down.".

Now that astronomers may have found the first such merger, "I can't wait to find more," Karambelkar remarked. "Upcoming telescopes like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Vera Rubin Observatory will be very useful in discovering many more such events.".

Recent findings suggest that the scientists detailed their findings Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020.

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

In a recent development, those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

A Syrian who arrived in Germany as a refugee in 2015 has won a mayoral election in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.

Sources indicate that ryyan Alshebl, who left his hometown of As Suwayda in Syria eight years ago, ran as an independent in the municipality of Ostelsheim. He won 55.41% of the votes on Sunday, beating two German candidates, Marco Strauss and Mathias Fey.

Locals cheered the 29-year-old when he welcomed his win, a victory he described as “sensational,” German local broadcaster SWR reported Monday.

“Today, Ostelsheim sent an example for broad-mindedness and cosmopolitanism for the whole of Germany,” he mentioned, according to to German public broadcaster ZDF. “That’s not something that can be taken for granted in a conservative, rural area.”.

Alshebl’s first call after his victory was to his mother in Syria, who was thrilled with the news, SWR reported.

Industry observers note that the Association of Municipalities of Baden-Württemberg mentioned Alshebl is the first man with Syrian roots to run for and win a mayor’s office. He will start his role in June.

'You are not a refugee.' Roma refugees fleeing war in Ukraine say they are suffering discrimination and prejudice.

Sources indicate that ostelsheim residents have welcomed their incoming mayor. “The fairy tale has come true, and the right man has become our mayor,” Annette Keck, who lives in the village, told SWR.

Strauss, one of his opponents, congratulated Alshebl. “I wish you good luck and at the same time ask for support for Mr. Alshebl, for our shared Ostelsheim,” he said on Facebook.

The state’s Integration Minister Manne Lucha remarked that Alshebl’s victory showed that diversity is a natural part of Baden-Württemberg. “I would be very pleased if Ryyan Alshebl’s election encourages more people with a migration history to run for political office,” he said.

In a recent development, not everyone has been so warm to the 29-year-old. ZDF reported the Syrian received hateful comments on the campaign trail.

The young politician went from house to house, promoting his election program, and “the experiences were predominantly positive,” but there was also a minority of far-right fringe voters in Ostelsheim that did not want to accept him due to his Syrian roots, Alshebl told ZDF.

Born to a schoolteacher and agricultural engineer in Syria, Alshebl described his life as carefree until the age of 20, according to his campaign website.

Recent findings suggest that at the time, protests against the Syrian government that began in 2011 soon devolved into chaotic war. The fighting and later rise of ISIS forced 10.6 million people from home by late 2015 – about half of Syria’s pre-war population.

Alshebl faced the dilemma of being drafted for military service with the Syrian army or leaving the country, according to his website.

While many Syrians were displaced internally or fled to countries in the region, others like Alshebl made the dangerous journey to Europe. He was 21 years old at the time, and mentioned he crossed from Turkey to the Greek island of Lesbos in a rubber dinghy.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel had implemented a brief open-door policy in 2015 that saw the country take in about 1.2 million asylum seekers in the following years, including Alshebl.

Recent findings suggest that they were welcomed into British homes. Celebrating their first Christmas together, Ukrainians wonder if that hospitality will last.

The move sparked a backlash in Germany and the sudden growth of the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the wake of summer 2015.

Once in Germany, Alshebl lived close to Ostelsheim and mentioned at the time he felt “there is only one thing you can do: get back on your feet swiftly and start investing in your own future quickly.”.

Recent findings suggest that for the last seven years he worked in the administration of Althengstett town hall, in a neighboring town. He drew from his experience, he said in his campaign, and made digital access to to public administration services one of priorities. Flexible childcare and climate protections are also on his agenda.

Alshebl, who is a member of the Green Party and now has German citizenship, pledged during his campaign that once elected as mayor he would move to Ostelsheim.

  • This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League.

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

Marlon Gomes (Shakhtar Donetsk).

Josko Gvardiol (Manchester City).

Alessandro Bastoni* (Inter Milan).

Cristian Martinez (Slovan Bratislava).

Alexis Mac Allister (Liverpool).

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card.

Tech Report: Tristan Thompson Reveals His “Home Run” Investment in Anthropic AI

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At least, that’s true when it comes to his early investment in Anthropic AI, the artificial intelligence firm that saw major financial wins this week when it went public and sold $81.3 billion worth of stock shares, according to CNBC.
  • Noting he's “happy" about the company's recent successes, Thompson told Yahoo Finance that he got involved in the tech brand over two years ago while visiting San Francisco as part of his NBA schedule when he was playing for the Cleveland Cavaliers.
